title: The stoning
hookLine: pebbles thrown at pillars where Ibrahim rejected Shaytan's whispers

cards: Small stones. That's what the morning after Muzdalifah comes down to. On the day of sacrifice, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ reaches a pillar in the valley at Mina and throws pebbles at it, one at a time.

On the road before, he asks Ibn Abbas to pick some up for him. Ibn Abbas brings back little ones, the kind you could flick between a finger and a thumb. The Prophet shakes them in his hand and says: like these.
Not rocks. Nothing bigger to make a point. Today's word is the place those small stones are thrown.

teach.b: Jamarat: the pillars of Mina, and the rite of stoning them. Start with what the Prophet did. In Jabir's account in Sahih Muslim, he comes to the jamrah, throws seven small pebbles, and says Allahu akbar with each one.
A throw, and God is greater. Next, the size, and a warning.
In the report from Ibn Abbas in al-Nasa'i, after like these, the Prophet adds: beware of going to extremes in religion, because extremes destroyed those who came before.
The pebbles are small on purpose. The rite doesn't need anger to work. Then, the story people tell.
A report attributed to Ibn Abbas says that at these spots Shaytan appeared to Ibrahim, trying to turn him from what God had asked, and Ibrahim drove him off with stones.
It isn't in the Qur'an; it's a report kept in the hadith books, and the tradition remembers the stoning through it. Last, what the rite is for.

Aisha is reported, in Sunan Abi Dawud, to have said that the circling of the House, the walk between Safa and Marwa, and the stoning were set up for the remembrance of God. So the target isn't really the pillar.
The Qur'an's closing surah names the enemy: "the sneaking whisperer, Who whispereth in the hearts of mankind." You met that whisper back on day twenty-six. It doesn't shout.
It suggests. And the answer the rite rehearses is just as quiet: a small stone, a clear refusal, God is greater. Pilgrims do it again in the days that follow.
A whisper comes back, so the refusal comes back too.

how: On the day of sacrifice pilgrims throw small pebbles at the pillar called Jamrat al-Aqabah at Mina, saying Allahu akbar with each, and on the following days they stone all the pillars.

o: large rocks thrown in anger at a statue of Shaytan
the pillars at Mina where pilgrims throw small pebbles
the tents pilgrims sleep in during the days at Mina

p: the Prophet's word on the stones
set up for the remembrance of God

s: the Qur'an tells the story of Ibrahim stoning Shaytan at Mina
it's a report attributed to Ibn Abbas, kept in the hadith books, not the Qur'an.
the Prophet said Allahu akbar with each pebble
Jabir's account: a takbir with every throw.
the Prophet chose small pebbles and warned against going to extremes in religion.

games.q: you're picking up stones for the Prophet to throw at the pillar. which do you bring?
o: the biggest rocks you can carry.
small pebbles you could flick with a finger.
a shoe, to really make a point.
games.why: Ibn Abbas brings small pebbles, the Prophet says like these, and warns against going to extremes in religion.

practice: Let one familiar thought come up, the quiet one that nudges you toward something you'd rather not do, and don't fight it; just name it, plainly, as a whisper.
If you pray, say a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim, the words Muslims use to seek refuge from Shaytan; if not, picture a small stone in your hand, and set the thought down with it.

wordCard.voice: Jamarat. The pillars at Mina where pilgrims throw small pebbles, a takbir with each, remembering Ibrahim's refusal. Today's word.

orig.note: the pillars of Mina, and the stoning done at them.

carryVoice: Your line: reject the whisper. A small stone, a clear no, no anger needed. Rest well.

sources.ref: report of Ibn Abbas on Ibrahim and Shaytan at the jamarat (al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak; al-Bayhaqi)
